title: The news: gathering and delivering
subtitle: scoop, deadline, column inches, hit the headlines
summary: Talk about how journalists gather and publish news - press conferences, soundbites and sources at one end, scoops, spin and libel at the other.

lesson.heading: Types of journalism
lesson.text: There are several kinds: **print journalism** (newspapers and magazines), **broadcast journalism** (radio and TV), **online journalism** (news websites) and, increasingly, **citizen journalism**, where ordinary citizens use social media to report, photograph and share news with others.

examples.text: She moved from **print journalism** into television.
Social media have encouraged the development of **citizen journalism**.

lesson.heading: Where stories come from
lesson.text: Journalists may get stories from **pressure groups** - people trying to influence what others think about an issue - who want to **air their views** in public. Journalists also attend **press conferences**, meetings where politicians give information to the press and answer questions, and where someone may **issue a statement** or a **press release**.

examples.text: The President will be holding a **press conference** this afternoon.
Politicians are always ready to **air their views** in the press.
The minister **issued a statement** but refused to take questions.

lesson.heading: Publicity, soundbites and sources
lesson.text: A person seeking **publicity** - wanting to reach a wider audience - will try to include a **soundbite** in what they say: a short, memorable phrase that will be repeated in news bulletins. Journalists hunt for stories by **tapping** useful **sources**, making use of people who regularly provide news, and by **monitoring** (regularly checking) international news agencies. **Paparazzi** is an informal, sometimes disapproving word for press photographers who chase celebrities.

examples.text: Politicians are usually not slow to seek **publicity**.
The whole speech was written round a single **soundbite**.
He built his career on **tapping sources** nobody else had.

lesson.heading: How much space a story gets
lesson.text: The more important a story is, the more **airtime** it will achieve - the minutes given to it on radio or TV - and the more **column inches** it will be given in the paper. In other words, the more **coverage**, or media attention, it will receive.

examples.text: The story received a lot of **airtime** on the radio.
The floods took up more **column inches** than any other story this week.
The story has had a lot of **media attention**.

lesson.heading: Producing the paper
lesson.text: Journalists produce **copy**, the written material, which has to be ready for a **deadline**. When everything is ready, the newspaper **goes to press**. Previous issues are **back copies**, usually accessible in an online **archive**.

examples.text: We had to produce all our **copy** to very tight **deadlines**.
The paper **went to press** at two in the morning.
I have to find some articles from some **back copies** of The Times.

lesson.heading: Scoops, breaking and headlines
lesson.text: A story found in only one newspaper is an **exclusive** or a **scoop**. Every paper hopes to **run** a story nobody else has. A major story **hits the headlines** on the day it is published; at that moment the story **breaks**, or becomes public knowledge.

examples.text: The TV news yesterday **ran** a story about my favourite singer.
The story **broke** last night when it was the first item on the TV news.
The scandal surrounding her uncle **hit the headlines** on her wedding day.

lesson.heading: Disapproving words about the press
rows: an informal word for a newspaper, suggesting it is not of high quality
papers more interested in crime and sex than in serious news
put a gloss / spin on a story
present it in your own way, to suit your own view
publishing an untrue written story that damages someone's reputation
damaging someone's reputation, in writing (libel) or in speech (slander)
lesson.note: Papers also make ordinary events sound dramatic with words like heroic and triumph, when the occurrence - the happening or event - is quite ordinary.

lesson.text: Media is a plural noun: the media are blamed for a number of social problems. It is also used as an adjective - media coverage, media hype, media attention.

exercises.prompt: Match the two parts of these collocations.
When I started out as a junior reporter, we had to produce all our ___ to very tight deadlines.
exercises.explanation: Copy is the uncountable word for the material a journalist writes.

exercises.prompt: We had to make sure the copy was all in place before the paper went to press, so we worked to very tight ___ .
exercises.hint: (plural: the times work must be finished by)
exercises.explanation: A deadline is the time by which the copy must be ready; the one thing a journalist must not miss.

exercises.prompt: It's easy to find old articles because most newspapers have an online ___ you can access.
exercises.explanation: Back copies - previous issues - are usually kept in an online archive.

exercises.prompt: People expect a lot more photos of celebrities these days, which is why we rely on the ___ so much.
exercises.explanation: Paparazzi is an informal, often disapproving word for photographers who chase public figures.

exercises.prompt: Now we publish online, so a story can appear a few minutes after it ___ .
exercises.explanation: When a story breaks it becomes public knowledge.

exercises.prompt: Every news report inevitably puts its own ___ on events.
exercises.hint: (presents them its own way; also gloss)
exercises.explanation: To put a spin or gloss on a story is to present it in your own way.

exercises.prompt: The floods took up more ___ inches in the papers than any other story this week.
exercises.explanation: Column inches measure the space a story is given in print.

exercises.prompt: Which word best completes this sentence? 'Politicians are usually not slow to seek ___ .'
exercises.explanation: To seek publicity is to want to reach a wider audience; coverage and airtime are what the media give you.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes this sentence? 'Unfortunately, muggings are an everyday ___ in this part of town.'
exercises.explanation: An occurrence is simply a happening or event; triumph is the dramatic word papers prefer.

exercises.prompt: 'Any newspaper does all it can to prevent being sued for libel.' Which phrase means the same as libel here?
exercises.explanation: Libel is written defamation of character; slander is the spoken kind.

exercises.statement: If you call a newspaper a rag, you are praising the quality of its journalism.
exercises.explanation: A rag is an informal word suggesting the paper is not of high quality - you would never use it when applying for a job there.

exercises.prompt: Put this sentence about a big story in order.
exercises.answer: The story hit the headlines on her wedding day
exercises.explanation: A major story hits the headlines on the day it is published.
